## Goals

-   Extend simple regression to multiple predictors
-   Fit and interpret an ANCOVA (categorical + continuous predictor)
-   Practice basic model comparison

## Setup



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
data(trees)
```
:::



## Multiple regression



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m1 <- lm(Volume ~ Girth + Height, data = trees)
summary(m1)
```

::: callout-note
## Exercise 1

Compare this model's R² to the simple `Volume ~ Girth` model from Week 9's tutorial. Did adding `Height` meaningfully improve the fit? Use `anova(m_simple, m1)` to formally compare them (fit `m_simple` first).
:::

## ANCOVA: categorical + continuous predictor

We'll simulate a dataset where plant height depends on both a continuous covariate (starting size) and a categorical treatment — a common design in biology.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(7)
n <- 40
ancova_data <- tibble(
  treatment = rep(c("Control", "Fertilizer"), each = n / 2),
  start_height = runif(n, 5, 15),
  final_height = 2 + 1.1 * start_height +
    ifelse(treatment == "Fertilizer", 4, 0) +
    rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)
)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(ancova_data, aes(start_height, final_height, color = treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Final height vs. starting height, by treatment](week10-tutorial_files/figure-html/fig-ancova-1.png){#fig-ancova width=672}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_ancova <- lm(final_height ~ start_height + treatment, data = ancova_data)
summary(m_ancova)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
lm(formula = final_height ~ start_height + treatment, data = ancova_data)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-2.4858 -0.8144 -0.0333  0.9348  2.5330 

Coefficients:
                    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)          1.83801    0.66225   2.775   0.0086 ** 
start_height         1.13397    0.06569  17.263  < 2e-16 ***
treatmentFertilizer  3.95701    0.41434   9.550 1.59e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.266 on 37 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.932,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.9284 
F-statistic: 253.7 on 2 and 37 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
```


:::
:::



::: callout-note
## Exercise 2

In your own words, explain what the `treatment` coefficient represents in this model, and why controlling for `start_height` matters — what would happen to your conclusions if you ignored it and just compared `final_height` between groups with a t-test?
:::

## Checking for an interaction

ANCOVA assumes the slopes are parallel across groups (no treatment-by-covariate interaction). Always check this.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_interaction <- lm(final_height ~ start_height * treatment, data = ancova_data)
anova(m_ancova, m_interaction)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: final_height ~ start_height + treatment
Model 2: final_height ~ start_height * treatment
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
1     37 59.331                           
2     36 55.472  1    3.8589 2.5043 0.1223
```


:::
:::



::: callout-note
## Exercise 3

Is the interaction term significant? What would it mean, biologically, if it were? Then design a scenario (2–3 sentences) — a real or hypothetical biology dataset — where you'd genuinely expect treatment effects to depend on a covariate like starting size or age.
:::
